note_fixes: Replace Exodus 22:22–27 with two shorter passages: Exodus 22:21–22 (note: “You must not mistreat any widow or orphan”) and Exodus 22:27 (note: “And if he cries out to Me, I will hear, for I am compassionate”). Six verses of lending, interest and the pledged cloak are longer than the concept needs, and 22:21 is the verse that supplies the foreigner the name promises (22:22–27 has no foreigner).
concepts.why: Secular/academic reader and the passage-length rule: the six-verse passage carries creditor and cloak law the concept does not use, and the name's third term (foreigner) is in 22:21, which the passage does not include.

Biblical-theological and secular readers: the other six verses are accounts of Jesus moved with compassion. Mark 5:19 is Jesus telling a man what 'the Lord' (God, on one reading; Jesus, on another) has done and the 'mercy He has shown', a different word and a different subject. Keeping it settles who 'the Lord' is, and it does not say that He had compassion on them. The concept stands on six.

concepts.name: Our transgressions removed, cast into the depths of the sea
concepts.why: Secular/academic reader, name against passages: 'As far as the east is from the west' is the image of Ps 103:12 alone. Isa 38:17 (behind Your back), Jer 50:20 (guilt searched for and not found) and Mic 7:19 (depths of the sea) use other images, so the name says more than three of the four passages. A name in the texts' words that all four support: 'Our transgressions removed, cast into the depths of the sea' (Ps 103:12 'removed'; Isa 38:17 and Mic 7:19 'cast'). Alternative: 'Your sins cast behind Your back, into the depths of the sea'.

concepts.name: He heals and binds up their wounds
concepts.why: Secular/academic reader, name against passages: 'He has wounded us' is said by Hos 6:1, Deut 32:39 and Isa 30:26 only. Ps 147:3, Jer 30:17 and Jer 33:6 speak of healing wounds and say nothing of God inflicting them. The name takes Ps 147:3's words, which all six passages support. The three that name the wounding keep it in their own words.

Jewish reader of the Hebrew Bible and secular scholar: the concept is named in the words of Isa 55:3 ('My loving devotion promised to David') and holds six verses that say it. Acts 13:34 does not say 'loving devotion' (it says 'holy and sure blessings'), shares only 'promised to David' (the drafter's own account says so), and its verse is the resurrection claim ('God raised Him from the dead'). Placed under Isa 55:3's name it reads as Paul's answer to the Davidic promise, which is the fulfilment framing the site avoids. The concept stands on six verses, and Acts 13:34 can live in a New Testament outline.

secondary_or_links: Same sub-theme named twice: concepts 43 ('I will restore them because I have compassion on them') and 44 ('I will restore you from captivity'). Deut 30:3, Jer 33:26 and Ezek 39:25 in 43 are each a 'restore from captivity' verse, which is what 44 collects, so they are one promise with the hinge word 'compassion' added. Merge them, or keep 43 only for verses where compassion and restoring occur in the same verse and move Deut 30:3, Jer 33:26 and Ezek 39:25 into 44, which then gets 'compassion' as a second link. Closer than the rest, but not the same sub-theme: 23/24 (God's anger not forever / remembering mercy in wrath) and 44/45 (restore from captivity / gather from the nations).

Section C 'Restoration → Shepherd': Luke 15:5 does not say shepherd, restore or gather (it says he 'joyfully puts it on his shoulders'). Swap for a verse that names the shepherd, for example Matthew 9:36 ('like sheep without a shepherd') or Isaiah 40:11, so the label rests on the verse's own words.

Concept 31, Luke 23:34 (secular/academic reader, a note and no change required): the first sentence ('Father, forgive them…') is absent from several early manuscripts and is bracketed in critical editions. It is a prayer that God forgive, not a person forgiving. Its inclusion is defensible; if the site marks disputed readings elsewhere, mark it here.

Links: no change. The Israel/church pairs (concepts 27, 42, 54, 55) are set side by side with no name or note saying who is who, and I found no concept name or note that says an Old Testament passage is fulfilled in or points to a New Testament one. The last core concept (57) is the theme's own words of hope, and the dark words stand in earlier concepts (9, 14, 25, 26, 42), so nothing is softened to make room.
